list.listitem: Listeriosis is predominantly a food-borne illness. Pregnant and immunocompromised persons should avoid eating foods at high risk for transmitting Listeria, including soft cheeses, raw milk, and unheated processed meats. C
Consider listeriosis in neonates with fever, sepsis, or meningitis, in adults with CNS infection, and in outbreaks of foodborne illness. Confirm diagnosis by culture of blood or CSF. C
Febrile infants less than 28 days of age should receive empiric IV ampicillin to cover for Listeria, in addition to either a third-generation cephalosporin or aminoglycoside. B
CDC recommends IV ampicillin + gentamicin for 14 to 21 days for all exposed, symptomatic persons. C
Even with appropriate antimicrobial treatment, invasive Listeriosis carries a mortality rate of 20%. B

background.definition: Listeriosis is a systemic infection that presents clinically as sepsis or meningitis in immunocompromised patients, neonates, and the elderly. If contracted during pregnancy, it is associated with preterm delivery, stillbirth, spontaneous abortion, or severe infection in the neonate. It is caused by listeria monocytogenes, a gram positive facultative anaerobic bacterium.

list.listitem: An estimated 2500 cases occur each year in the United States, 500 of which result in death.
Incidence of meningitis attributed to Listeria is 0.2 per 100,000 people.
Listeria monocytogenes accounts for 8% of cases of bacterial meningitis in the United States.
In 2010, it is estimated that listeriosis resulted in 23,150 illnesses and 5463 deaths worldwide.
Monocytogenes, a gram positive rod.
See table below for risk factors.

Monocytogenes has been isolated from soil as well as the intestinal tracts of animals and asymptomatic individuals. Transmission occurs through consumption of unpasteurized milk, soft cheeses, and ready-to-eat meats such as cold cuts and hot dogs.
Monocytogenes can cross intestinal, placental, and blood-brain barriers.
Neonatal listeriosis is thought to be perinatally acquired.

Incubation period for invasive disease varies is 8 days on average with a range of 1-67 days, but varies by clinical form of the disease. The median incubation period is 27.5 days for pregnancy-associated disease; 9 for meningitis; 2 days for bacteremia and 1 day for gastroenteritis.
Pregnant and immunocompromised patients should avoid eating foods at high risk for transmitting Listeria, including soft cheeses, raw milk, and unheated processed meats. C
Consider listeriosis in the differential diagnosis of neonates with fever, sepsis, or meningitis, in adults with CNS infection, and in outbreaks of foodborne illness. C
No reliable clinical method exists to definitively separate Listeria infection from other infections that cause fever and constitutional symptoms. C
Definitive diagnosis can only be established by culture of sterile body fluids such as blood or CSF. C
There are no reliable history or physical examination findings that distinguish listerial infections from other infections causing fever, sepsis, and meningitis.

Listeriosis should be strongly considered in the differential diagnosis in the following settings: Neonatal fever, sepsis, or meningitis. Meningitis or parenchymal brain infection in patients with hematologic malignancies, AIDS, organ transplantation, or corticosteroid immunosuppression. Meningitis or parenchymal brain infection in adults older than 50 years of age. Simultaneous infection of the meninges and brain parenchyma, or subcortical brain abscess. Fever during pregnancy, particularly during the third trimester (in the absence of underlying immunosuppressive illness or treatment, pregnant women virtually never develop listerial CNS infections). Blood, CSF, or other normally sterile specimens reported to have "diptheroids" on Gram stain or culture. Foodborne outbreak of febrile gastroenteritis when routine cultures fail to identify a pathogen.
Diagnosis requires isolation of L. monocytogenes from sterile clinical specimens and identification through standard microbiologic techniques.

Isolates are most commonly identified from blood and CSF; however, stereotactic biopsy of a brain abscess is another alternative in patients with parenchymal involvement seen on imaging. This approach may be useful in patients at high risk for herniation from lumbar puncture or those with inconclusive CSF findings.

Serodiagnosis of listeriosis by measuring antibodies to listeriolysin O have been useful in identifying infected individuals with noninvasive disease such as gastroenteritis during foodborne outbreaks.
PCR is increasingly the preferred test to diagnose listeriosis.
Monocytogenes, while technically rod shaped, may appear coccoid on Gram stain and can be mistaken for pneumococci or diptheroids. Gram stain alone is insufficient for ruling out L. monocytogenes.
Recognize patients at risk for invasive listeriosis: febrile neonates, immunocompromised patients, or adults over 50 presenting with sepsis or meningitis.
Obtain cultures and Gram stains of blood and CSF. A negative Gram stain does not rule out listeriosis, though.
Begin empiric antibiotic treatment with meningitis doses of ampicillin. Treatment in all groups with confirmed listeriosis is continued for a minimum of 3 weeks.
Neonate less than 28 days old presenting with sepsis: add aminoglycoside such as gentamicin; if meningitis is suspected, add third-generation cephalosporin instead of an aminoglycoside.
Neonate 28 to 90 days old with a septic appearance: consider ampicillin in addition to either gentamicin or a third-generation cephalosporin pending culture or CSF Gram stain results.
Adult over 50 presenting with meningitis: begin ampicillin plus a third-generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin.

Febrile infants less than 28 days of age should, as part of their workup for sepsis and meningitis, receive empiric IV ampicillin to cover for Listeria, in addition to either a third-generation cephalosporin or aminoglycoside. Ampicillin plus gentamicin is recommended by CDC for symptomatic, exposed persons. B
Adults over the age of 50 with meningitis should receive empiric IV ampicillin to cover for Listeria, in addition to a third-generation cephalosporin and vancomycin. C
Treatment should continue for a minimum of 3 weeks. C

Pregnant women who are symptomatic with a flu-like illness preceeded by diarrhea and other GI symptoms, and in whom no other etiology for their symptoms can be found, should be simultaneously tested and treated for presumptive Listeria. C

Ampicillin is the preferred first-line agent for the treatment of infections caused by L. monocytogenes. If using penicillin G, consider addition of an aminoglycoside. In vivo and in vitro data suggest that ampicillin is superior to penicillin in the treatment of CNS listeriosis.

The beta-lactams are bacteriostatic for Listeria. Based on in vitro and animal models, a common practice is to add gentamicin to ampicillin for those with severe T-cell impairment and in all cases of meningitis and endocarditis. For those intolerant of penicillins, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as a single agent is thought to be the best alternative. Meningitis doses should be used for all patients even in the absence of CNS or CSF abnormalities due to the high affinity of Listeria for the CNS.

One study suggests that ampicillin plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole may be more efficacious than ampicillin plus gentamicin. Other less studied alternatives include meropenem or linezolid plus rifampin.

Febrile infants less than 28 days of age should, as part of their workup for sepsis and meningitis, receive empiric IV ampicillin to cover for Listeria, in addition to either a third-generation cephalosporin or aminoglycoside.
Adults over the age of 50 with meningitis should receive empiric IV ampicillin to cover for Listeria, in addition to a third-generation cephalosporin and vancomycin.

Treatment of Listeria with ampicillin should continue for a minimum of 3 weeks' duration. In a neonate, treatment should continue for 3 weeks or 2 weeks after the first sterile CSF culture, whichever is longer. Treatment of at least 5 to 6 weeks is recommended in the context of localized CNS involvement.
Surgery may be required in patients with cerebral abscesses and neurologic deficits, as well as for hydrocephalus in patients with meningitis/meningoencephalitis.
Hospitalization is required for neonatal patients with fever or signs of sepsis, patients with serious illness, and patients with any CNS symptomatology.
Fever of unknown origin in a pregnant woman should prompt urgent referral to a hospital or specialist consultation regarding diagnosis, treatment, and fetal status.
Even with appropriate antimicrobial treatment, invasive listeriosis carries a mortality rate of 20%. B

Because of increased susceptibility of patients over 50 years to listerial infections, all patients with meningitis in this age group should be treated with ampicillin in addition to a third-generation cephalosporin and vancomycin.

One-third of listeriosis cases occur in pregnant women, who may experience a flu-like illness or gastroenteritis; more serious clinical manifestations affect their newborns, including sepsis, meningitis, preterm birth, or stillbirth.
Fever of unknown origin in a pregnant woman should be evaluated urgently at a hospital with specialist consultation.
It occurs most often in the 3rd trimester and rarely in the first. First line treatment is also ampicillin.

Neonates presenting with fever, sepsis, or meningitis should have blood and CSF cultures drawn and should be empirically treated with ampicillin to cover for a potential Listeria infection, in addition to an aminoglycoside or third-generation cephalosporin.
